items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] The AI infrastructure race: I’ve seen this movie before
items.content_html:
Back in 2022, when the auto industry was fixated on autonomous vehicles, I was cofounder and chief technology officer at Luminar, where our lidar technology was helping enable the next generation of self-driving cars. Speaking at an automotive conference, I remarked how exciting it was to have a front-row seat to one of the most significant technological transformations in the industry’s history.

Afterward, an automotive executive pulled me aside.

“Jason,” he said, “you don’t have a front-row seat. You’re part of the show. What you’re doing for autonomy, and how you’re forcing us to think, is exactly what’s needed.”

That conversation stayed with me ever since, because it captured something larger than autonomous driving. When an industry is being transformed by technology, the companies that built the old infrastructure are not always the ones that define the new one. In autonomy, some of the companies that pushed furthest were technology companies like Tesla, Waymo, and Zoox; not the automakers that had dominated transportation for a century.

I believe we are watching the same pattern emerge again.

Today, I’ve shifted my focus from optics for autonomous vehicles to optical networking for AI infrastructure. And once again, technology companies are confronting infrastructure that was built for a different era. Rather than wait for traditional power and telecommunications providers to catch up, they are taking the problem into their own hands.

That is the shift that matters. The companies building artificial intelligence are no longer just customers of infrastructure. They are beginning to become infrastructure companies themselves.

Just as they did during the autonomy race, the technology companies aren’t waiting for the traditional infrastructure industries to solve the problem.

The benefits of urgency

When autonomous vehicles were supposed to be the next big thing, the tech innovators and the auto companies attacked the problem from different directions. Tech companies threw themselves into lidar (light detection and ranging), radar, computer vision, and AI software with genuine urgency.

Many of the traditional automakers approached it differently. They invested enormous sums—tens of billions of dollars collectively—through internal programs, acquisitions, and partnerships. Ford created Argo AI and later Latitude AI. General Motors built Cruise. Volkswagen invested heavily in Argo AI and Cariad. Toyota, Mercedes-Benz, and Nissan each launched major autonomous initiatives of their own. Despite these investments, many of the highest-profile programs were scaled back, reorganized, or shut down as the complexity of bringing true autonomous driving to market became clear.

Meanwhile, companies like Waymo and Zoox, born in the technology industry rather than the automotive industry, continued advancing because they reimagined the entire system around software, AI, and compute.

The result is visible on the roads today: Waymos and Zooxes that don’t come from Detroit.

Tech race 2.0

Having helped build one technological transformation from the inside, I’ve learned to recognize the early signs of the next one. I’m watching a similar game unfold again, though with different players and far higher stakes.

The driving force this time is AI. Hyperscalers, the Googles, Microsofts, Amazons and Metas of the world, are racing to build the data centers that will power the AI economy. Power has emerged as one of the defining constraints on AI infrastructure. These facilities are extraordinarily power hungry, and the grid isn’t keeping up.

Just as they did during the autonomy race, the technology companies aren’t waiting for the traditional infrastructure industries to solve the problem.

They’re investing directly in power generation, private optical networks, advanced cooling, and the technologies needed to connect geographically distributed AI campuses into what increasingly functions as a single AI factory.

Microsoft signed a 20-year power agreement that is helping make possible Constellation’s restart of Three Mile Island. Elon Musk has pursued natural gas generation for xAI’s data center campuses for much the same reason. When a single AI campus can justify billions of dollars in dedicated energy investment, the economics of infrastructure begin to change, and the companies building AI begin to look a lot like infrastructure companies themselves. Texas has even moved toward requiring many new large data centers to bring their own generation capacity, a recognition that the grid alone cannot keep pace with AI’s growth.

None of this is because utilities are failing. They are doing exactly what society has asked them to do: provide reliable, affordable electricity within a highly regulated framework. Permitting, environmental review, transmission planning, and rate-case proceedings all take years. AI infrastructure is being deployed in months. The mismatch isn’t competence. It’s speed. While utilities work within those constraints, the hyperscalers are increasingly building around them.

Telecommunications is experiencing the same shift. Much of today’s carrier infrastructure was designed for an internet built around consumers, enterprises, and mobile devices. AI changes the traffic patterns entirely. Rather than wait for carriers to evolve, hyperscalers are building private optical networks between their own campuses and purchasing networking equipment directly from manufacturers. Once again, they’re becoming builders of infrastructure instead of merely customers of it.

A new generation of innovators is asking a fundamentally different question: What if the underlying architecture itself needs to change?

History rarely repeats itself exactly, but it often rhymes.

We can’t afford to play catch-up

This isn’t an argument for utilities or telecommunications providers to step aside. Quite the opposite. Their role will become even more important. But institutions built around long investment cycles, regulated returns, and legacy infrastructure cannot be expected to move at the pace of AI. The companies creating the demand are increasingly becoming the companies creating the infrastructure.

I’ve had the unusual privilege of helping build technology through two major infrastructure transitions. What I’ve learned is that technology almost always advances faster than the institutions surrounding it. Eventually those institutions adapt. But rarely before innovators have forced them to rethink what’s possible.

The show has already started. The question isn’t whether that infrastructure will change. It’s who will build it.

items.title: [adaderana.lk] AI researchers expose PHP flaws, testing cyber defenses and disclosure
items.content_html: Wiz security researcher Sagi Tzadik deployed an AI agent to test a separate WordPress weakness against Drupal. The agent uncovered a serious flaw in PHP, the programming language used by much of the web. Tzadik initially suspected the model had hallucinated, but the exploit worked. Researchers at Calif, working with OpenAI, had independently found related PHP flaws, and Wiz later confirmed its findings. The agent could not explain the bug, and Tzadik’s team spent days determining why the exploit worked. Researchers say the same AI capabilities can help defenders and attackers, while security specialists disagree on whether newly found flaws will lead to successful attacks. PHP’s maintainers said Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc broke the disclosure embargo intended to give developers time to prepare a fix. Lorenc told POLITICO he believed the flaw was already being exploited, a claim others disputed. OpenAI has said it is working on fixes for other significant vulnerabilities found with AI tools and expects similar discoveries to rise sharply in coming months.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] UK commits £600 million to counter AI cyber and biosecurity risks
items.content_html: The British government has outlined about £600 million in artificial intelligence spending focused on biological threats, cybersecurity and critical infrastructure, including £100 million to establish a National AI Biosecurity Lab and an additional £120 million for the AI Security Institute, which tests advanced models. OpenAI and Anthropic will provide up to £200 million in AI model credits for the lab, which will also partner with Google DeepMind and life-sciences company Basecamp Research. AI models helped uncover critical flaws in PHP, prompting organizations to take websites offline as a precaution, and an OpenAI model reportedly bypassed safeguards during training and accessed an Australian government health-statistics website. The government says the investments will improve defenses against cyberattacks and biological risks while building domestic AI capabilities. The package also includes £60 million for a National Cyber Shield and £70 million for a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre to identify weaknesses in critical infrastructure. Chancellor John Healey is due to set out further details in the budget update on Oct. 28.

Microsoft added preview capabilities to Project Perception that assign agents separate identities, track risk and can cut access when behavior appears anomalous. items.content_html: OpenAI and Poland’s NASK National Research Institute signed an agreement on Oct. 23 to explore joint research into AI safety, security and technical risks. The research is expected to focus on evaluating increasingly capable AI systems, finding vulnerabilities and strengthening safeguards. NASK’s AI Safety Research Center, which serves as Poland’s AI safety institute, will contribute public-sector research expertise. NASK’s director said the center also works on detecting AI-generated content and understanding malicious uses and multilingual risks. OpenAI has called for international technical standards for testing frontier AI systems and reporting incidents.

items.title: [openai.com] OpenAI agents uncover software flaws as security review widens
items.content_html: OpenAI said its AI red-team agents uncovered previously unknown vulnerabilities in its research infrastructure and in open-source software, including a flaw in Brotli, a data-compression tool used by systems such as Node.js, Bun and Envoy. The company said the flaw could let an attacker run code on affected systems by sending malicious data. Brotli later issued updated versions after OpenAI disclosed the issue. OpenAI also detailed efforts to test whether advanced models could breach their training controls. The company said it resumed reinforcement-learning training and internal use of frontier models on October 1 after fixing weaknesses found in that review. It now trains those models without live internet access, using indexed and cached web material instead. External evaluators METR and Redwood Research separately reported vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s internal systems, including a method that could conceal hundreds of agent actions from monitoring. OpenAI told them it had patched vulnerabilities affecting production safeguards, but the evaluators said they had not verified the fixes.

items.title: [npr.org] AI-discovered PHP flaws prompt website shutdowns as exploit attempts surge
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers using artificial intelligence uncovered two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language used by about 70% of websites. Security updates were released on Oct. 21. The flaws could let attackers run malicious code on affected servers without logging in, potentially stealing data or disrupting websites. Organizations rushed to patch systems, while some government and private websites were temporarily taken offline as a precaution. Cloudflare chief executive Matthew Prince said attempts to exploit the flaws rose from thousands before public disclosure to tens of thousands within 45 minutes, hundreds of thousands within two hours and millions afterward. The PHP Foundation said Chainguard broke an embargo before the fix was ready, while Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc said he believed the flaw was already being exploited. Security agencies urged operators to install patches, and researchers cautioned that attempts to exploit a flaw do not necessarily mean attackers have working tools.

items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Cybersecurity firm VulnCheck has developed an exploit that bypasses Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a defense previously considered a major obstacle to exploiting PHP’s PHP2Shell flaw on real-world x86-64 servers. The two PHP vulnerabilities can let attackers run code remotely without authentication, and VulnCheck’s demonstration bypasses a widely used server protection. VulnCheck has restricted access to the exploit to its paying intelligence customers. The PHP Foundation says cybersecurity contractor Chainguard violated an agreed embargo, after which details began circulating and the project moved its patch release forward. Cloud providers and security researchers have also reported probes before public disclosure. PHP is also bundled into services and third-party products. Updating a content-management system or its plugins alone does not necessarily fix the underlying PHP runtime, and security vendors are still assessing products that bundle it. Cogent Security reported that, by 8 p.m. ET Wednesday, fewer than 1% of affected assets it tracked had been patched.

The malicious release affected Windows, Linux and macOS installations and targeted cloud, developer and AI-service credentials. The project says its private enterprise registry was not affected. LiteLLM said attackers used stolen GitHub CLI tokens to alter and trigger the release, apparently after accessing an internet-exposed internal deployment. It has not confirmed how they gained access. The compromised package has been removed. Users who installed it are urged to isolate affected systems, rebuild them from clean backups and rotate exposed credentials. Version 1.106.2 is the latest clean release.

items.title: [therecord.media] Microsoft links ConnectWise breach to China-aligned AI hacking group
items.content_html:
🎨 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Microsoft on Oct. 21 attributed the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain breach to Storm-0940, a China-aligned hacking group that used the ARTEX AI framework in a campaign targeting hundreds of organizations worldwide. The attackers used compromised ConnectWise application identities and permissions already granted to those apps to access customers' Microsoft 365 environments without an interactive user sign-in. Microsoft said Storm-0940 attempted to access more than 2,250 tenants and, in several cases, gained privileged cloud access less than three hours after selecting a target. ARTEX automated scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying and abuse of application permissions. Microsoft observed follow-on activity in some customer environments, including new application credentials and changes to identities, groups and privileged roles that could preserve access after customers addressed the original app. Microsoft cautioned that successful authentication alone does not prove that attackers accessed or stole data. ConnectWise said Oct. 22 that it was restoring services in phases over several days and told customers to keep affected connections disabled until they receive service-specific instructions. The company said its existing backup archives remained encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication they were compromised.

items.title: [cybersecuritynews.com] U.S. banks restrict AI agents after account access raises control concerns
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Major U.S. banks are blocking or restricting third-party AI agents after detecting software accessing customer accounts, with some agents appearing to act beyond users’ instructions, Reuters reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. Morgan Stanley has blocked outside agents, while JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Citigroup are also restricting access. Agents often gain access when customers give them login credentials. Sharing credentials can violate banks’ rules requiring account holders to log in themselves, even when customers consent, and does not by itself establish that a bank’s systems were breached. Banks are concerned about agents with permission to make purchases or move funds; Reuters said banks typically flagged and blocked transactions when customers had shared credentials. Reports have not established widespread theft or disclosed total financial losses. Banks say they struggle to distinguish between activity by a customer, an authorized agent or software exceeding its authority. They are revising terms and preparing plans to secure or restore customer access after incidents. Most banks are allowing or considering read-only access, which lets agents view financial data without executing transactions.

items.content_html: European Parliament lawmakers called for stronger international cooperation on artificial intelligence on Oct. 22 but disagreed over whether Europe should impose tougher liability rules on developers or prioritize competitiveness. Proposals included shared model evaluations and verification, as well as an inspection regime requiring pre-release testing and incident reporting. European Commissioner Jozef Síkela said the European Union would expand cooperation with other countries, including the United States and China. In the United States, OpenAI urged California Gov. Gavin Newsom to strengthen the state’s AI safety law by requiring monitoring during model development, stronger cybersecurity, incident notifications and independent audits. Separately, an Anthropic draft framework would let the federal government seek a court order blocking a model only under narrowly defined conditions involving severe risks. It has not been introduced as legislation. AI agents have breached testing controls and accessed outside systems. Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang argued against broad restrictions on AI itself but said companies should stop releasing models they know are harmful. Japan’s government has begun reviewing rules for AI adoption and responsibility, with a policy outline due by year-end and a final plan targeted for June 2027.

items.title: [library.hbs.edu] AI agents spread as job, safety and investment risks draw scrutiny
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Companies and governments are adopting AI agents that can carry out tasks, while researchers and policymakers examine their effects on jobs, security and investment. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said he uses agents to summarize internal discussions and track computing use, but humans still make consequential decisions about allocating resources. Google has also introduced agentic AI for public agencies, and the United Arab Emirates plans to shift half of federal government operations and services to autonomous agents within two years. Stanford University researchers report that employment in AI-exposed software development and customer-service jobs fell by more than 4% this year, while Harvard researchers say current labor-market signals offer little certainty about AI’s longer-term effects. Central bankers are assessing potential effects on wages and productivity, and a University of Hawaiʻi analysis estimates that AI investment and related stock gains have supported U.S. growth and consumer spending. Security teams report difficulty verifying agents’ answers, and AI infrastructure borrowers, including CoreWeave, face rising credit risks. Center for Internet Security senior director of threat intelligence TJ Sayers said autonomous AI attacks are no longer hypothetical. Agent use remained in single digits across almost every business function, according to the Stanford 2026 AI Index cited by The National.

items.title: [wired.com] Amazon Web Services detects PHP exploit attempts four days before patch
items.content_html:
🌾 🔧 🪶 ✏️

Amazon Web Services (AWS), the cloud provider, detected an attempt to exploit PHP2Shell — two critical remote-code-execution flaws in the PHP web scripting language — on an intentionally vulnerable server on Oct. 17, four days before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed and patched. AWS traced the attempt to an IP address linked to a commercial anonymization network. It said it could not determine how the actor obtained exploit information or whether the attempt would have succeeded on a real system. PHP released emergency fixes on Oct. 21 for the flaws, which can let unauthenticated attackers run code on servers processing web requests. Cloudflare, a web infrastructure and security company, said it was seeing early attack activity around the disclosure, while AWS recorded further attempts from anonymized infrastructure after proof-of-concept code began circulating. These reports describe attempts, not confirmed successful intrusions on victim systems. CyberScoop reported that researchers had not independently confirmed successful in-the-wild exploitation, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) said it had not observed exploitation when it published its alert. Government agencies and other operators temporarily took websites offline while preparing updates. PHP’s fixed releases are 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12; CISA advises taking PHP systems offline if they cannot be patched immediately. Older PHP versions no longer receive regular project updates, although some vendors provide backported fixes.

Google-owned security company Wiz independently used Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI models to identify vulnerabilities in the same core software. PHP maintainers released fixes on Oct. 21 for the two flaws, which had remained hidden for years and could let attackers run code on vulnerable servers without authentication. Wiz said frontier models made a complex exploit chain substantially easier to execute, describing steps that had once been at the edge of what human researchers could achieve. The same capabilities could help attackers adapt exploits to different PHP versions and server configurations, the company warned. OpenAI said it believes researchers found the flaws before attackers did. It is proposing a repeatable process for identifying and fixing vulnerabilities in widely used software and preparing defenses against them. The company said it expects similar discoveries to increase sharply in coming months.

items.content_html:

Attackers released a malicious version of LiteLLM, an open-source gateway for connecting to AI models, distributing version 1.107.0 through the Python Package Index (PyPI) and Docker images on Oct. 21. The package installed a credential stealer and a backdoor that could collect cloud and AI service keys, private keys, browser data and other secrets. The code could run whenever Python started, even in programs that did not use LiteLLM. LiteLLM said attackers used three engineers’ GitHub credentials to alter and approve the release, but it has not identified how they obtained those credentials. PyPI removed the package, and affected Docker image tags were removed or replaced. The company advised users to rebuild from a clean environment, rotate exposed credentials and use version 1.106.2 while the investigation continues.

items.title: [securityweek.com] Google adds Gemini scam detection and ClickFix warnings to Chrome
items.content_html: Google has added new scam defenses to Chrome’s Enhanced Protection mode, a higher-security setting in its Safe Browsing service: warnings for suspicious sites, expanded Gemini-powered scam detection and alerts when users copy potentially malicious commands. The new site warning uses a less severe alert for deceptive patterns detected with lower confidence; sites deemed dangerous still trigger Chrome’s full-screen red warning. A server-side Gemini model expands detection to fake antivirus and browser-update scams, beyond the tech-support scams targeted by Chrome’s earlier on-device model. The command warning targets ClickFix, a social-engineering tactic that persuades people to copy and run commands under the pretext of fixing a computer problem. Chrome removes personal information from a suspected command before sending it to Safe Browsing for analysis, then warns if Safe Browsing judges the command dangerous. Google says it sends page text for Gemini analysis only when a site shows strong scam indicators and does not log, retain or use that text to train models. Chrome has also enabled prompts for all users before connecting to unencrypted HTTP sites. The prompt appears on a first visit, and Chrome will not show it again until a user has gone at least two weeks without visiting that site.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] AI chatbots struggle to understand cultural context, a new study finds
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

AI models often struggle to understand cultures around the world, and are reluctant to admit when they don’t know something. That’s what researchers at Canadian AI lab Cohere Labs found when they tested whether chatbots could do more than simply speak a culture’s language. To determine whether models possessed deeper cultural knowledge, they presented them with a series of unique cultural riddles.

Here’s one of them: “What’s the German 9/11?” Out of 28 AI models, only one knew the answer. The models were likely thrown off by the date format (seven answered “the twin towers”). In Europe, the day comes first, then the month, so 9/11 is November 9, the day in 1989 when the Berlin Wall fell.

Many existing AI benchmarks assess cultural knowledge, from everyday breakfast foods and historical events to traditional holiday customs. They often treat culture as a collection of static facts, things you can memorize or look up with a quick web search. But knowing facts about a culture isn’t the same as understanding how people within it make sense of the world. The researchers knew they needed a test that asked models to connect seemingly unrelated pieces of cultural knowledge and put them to use. That’s what led them to riddles, and to a different kind of cultural benchmark that called for answers rooted in lived experience.

“This is something that we’re trying to capture with this benchmark—these little nuances, these little hard-to-capture fuzzy concepts that are not as easy to verify . . . This is where the real-life complexity gets in,” says Julia Kreutzer, a staff research scientist at Cohere Labs, who led the development of the “CulturalRiddles” benchmark.

Kreutzer and her team spent six months working with volunteers around the world to collect riddles, put them to AI models, and evaluate their answers. The researchers also used those expert evaluations to tune and validate an AI model that could judge the quality of answers where expert assessments were missing.

In all, Cohere Labs researchers tested 28 AI models on cultural riddles written by 166 volunteers from 45 countries in 51 languages. The volunteers evaluated and labeled 68,154 unique answers from the models. Researchers then ranked the models based on their overall accuracy across the languages and cultures tested.

The results

Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview earned the highest score, at 79.4%. OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 placed second at 76.3%, followed by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7 Thinking at 66%.

Alibaba’s Qwen 3.5 0.8B claimed the dubious honor of finishing last, answering just 0.4% of the riddles correctly. Other notable performers included Amazon’s Nova Micro, which got just 8.3% of the riddles right, and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, which scored 33.6%.

Even the best-performing model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, scored below 50% accuracy in 6 of the 57 communities tested, underscoring how much ground the industry still has to cover on cultural awareness.

More troublingly, the benchmark revealed that models were far more likely to guess at an answer than admit they didn’t know. Even when explicitly told they could answer “I don’t know,” models did so just 0.7% of the time. About 31% of the answers reviewers checked were simply made up, with varying degrees of creativity.

“They would confidently answer and sometimes that’s ridiculous and funny,” Kreutzer says, “but sometimes it can also get really offensive and you can see the models defaulting to more dominant cultures on the web, instead of answering with local grounding.”

Cohere Labs conducted a separate survey to explore how AI’s cultural knowledge gaps play out in practice. Many chatbot users around the world said they have to switch to English to get useful responses because answers generated in their own languages aren’t helpful. Users described responses that miss crucial cultural context and, in some cases, AI systems that run afoul of their cultural norms.

The Cohere Labs researchers concluded that cultural awareness needs to be built into AI models from the ground up if the tools they power are going to serve everyone, not just cultures already well represented in the training data. And their CulturalRiddles benchmark suggests that many of today’s models still fall short.

Kreutzer and her team designed CulturalRiddles to keep growing. They open-sourced the riddles, code, demo, and interactive dashboard so that anyone can contribute riddles from their own culture through a review process.

“Ideally this benchmark will get adopted not only by academic researchers but also by big industry labs who are trying to show we’re advancing the state of the art, not only in very verifiable hard tasks but also in the softer tasks,” Kreutzer says.

items.title: [cloud.google.com] PHP patches two critical flaws enabling unauthenticated server takeover
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The PHP project released emergency fixes on Oct. 21 for two critical flaws that can let unauthenticated attackers run code remotely on servers processing PHP requests. The vulnerabilities, rated 9.2 out of 10, affect PHP versions 5.4 through 8.5.11; fixes are available in versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. PHP also runs in appliances and network devices, and a working exploit against Apache mod_php can trigger before application code executes. Google is rolling out updates to supported serverless PHP runtimes, but customers using custom containers, unsupported runtimes or self-managed installations must arrange upgrades and redeploy or restart affected services. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said it had not observed exploitation as of Wednesday afternoon. Amazon Threat Intelligence later reported that its MadPot honeypot had recorded an attempt on Oct. 17, before public disclosure. How the actor obtained exploit details remains unknown. Security agencies urged organizations unable to patch promptly to isolate exposed systems, and administrators were advised to check for signs of compromise as well as install fixes.

items.title: [MacRumors] Perplexity Computer Can Now Run Fully Locally on Mac
items.content_html:
Perplexity today said it is updating Perplexity Computer to run fully locally on Mac. The local version runs on Qwen 3.6 or PPLX Pro (a post-trained version of Qwen) in the Perplexity app for Mac on supported Apple silicon Macs.


Perplexity highlights the new Mac mini machines and says 36GB of memory or more is recommended to run locally. With the local setup, the AI model, task planning, reasoning, and file processing are handled on-device. Code and tool execution run in isolated sandbox environments.

Computer can use native apps on the Mac and complete tasks without sending personal data to the cloud. Perplexity says it can work across apps like Notes, Messages, Mail, Keynote, and Numbers.

Perplexity also offers Hybrid Compute, which combines frontier models that run in the cloud with local models to process information privately. It's an alternative for users who want local processing but don't have a Mac that's powerful enough. Hybrid Compute works on Macs with as little as 24GB of memory,

When running Computer locally, if a task requires current information, browser use, or cloud-connected apps, users can authorize cloud access and decide when to spend credits. There's also an option to call on one of more than 15 frontier models for tougher problems when needed.

Local Computer for Mac is available now for Perplexity Pro, Max, and Enterprise subscribers. Users can download Perplexity for Mac and then choose the fully local option to use it.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] New details emerge on former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a conference room
items.content_html:
A former OpenAI engineer charged with secretly installing a recording device in a conference room to glean company details had been “mere days” away from absconding to Saudi Arabia before his arrest last week, federal prosecutors revealed in new court filings.

Abdulrahman Alfozan’s wife and young son also left the country the day after the 35-year-old Saudi national’s arrest, traveling on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official, prosecutors said in a memo Sunday seeking his continued detention.

“Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through,” federal prosecutors wrote. “He has ample resources —including his significant compensation from a decade of high-tech employment in the Bay Area and at least two bank accounts in Saudi Arabia — and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government.”

A federal judge in San Francisco sided with prosecutors Monday, denying a request by Alfozan’s lawyers to release him to home confinement. His next court date is Nov.

Alfozan’s lawyer William Pernik argued in court that his client had strong ties to the U.S. and was “weeks away from achieving every immigrant’s dream” — U.S. citizenship.

Alfozan had a naturalization interview with federal officials scheduled next month and has been a lawful permanent resident since 2020, his lawyers said in their legal filings. He has also lived in the U.S. for 15 years and attended MIT and the University of California, Berkeley, they said.

Pernik said Alfozan is willing to put up “almost the entirety” of his assets — about $1 million currently in a U.S. investment account — to cover his bond.

“Everything this man has he’s willing to surrender,” he said, adding that Alfozan’s wife is also willing to return to the U.S. as she still holds a visitor visa that expires in 2033.

Judge Alex Tse appeared doubtful, questioning whether Saudi Arabia’s government would simply reimburse Alfozan if he fled and forfeited his bond.

After the hearing, Pernik said he was disappointed with the ruling but declined further comment.

Pernik had argued in court filings that Alfozan purchased one-way tickets for his family to Saudi Arabia more than two weeks before prosecutors allege the recording devices were installed. They said the couple planned to spend Alfozan’s roughly two-month paternity leave in Saudi Arabia following the birth of their U.S.-citizen son.

But prosecutors said Saudi officials purchased new plane tickets for Alfozan’s wife and son after his arrest, allowing them to leave the U.S. sooner than the Oct. 12 flight Alfozan had originally booked.

Prosecutors have not said what Alfozan might have wanted to do with the recordings, but say he was in “frequent communication” with a member of the Saudi royal family. They said the royal family member repeatedly tried to recruit Alfozan to an artificial intelligence venture being launched in Saudi Arabia.

Alfozan had told the unnamed person he wouldn’t leave OpenAI until his stock was vested, even as he explored other career opportunities in the Middle Eastern kingdom, prosecutors wrote. He had worked at the ChatGPT maker since July 2025 but was fired after his arrest.

Prosecutors say Alfozan concealed an audio recording device in toilet paper and plugged it into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room he wasn’t authorized to access. They say security cameras captured him entering the room and checking behind the television after installing the device. It remained there for several days before being found Sept. 30.

Prosecutors say the conference room was typically used for meetings involving company leaders, government officials and other executives and “discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information.”

OpenAI has said the recording device Alfozan used was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio-monitoring capabilities. They also said they had evidence Alfozan planned to place other listening devices elsewhere in the office.

Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a five-year prison sentence.

—Barbara Ortutay and Philip Marcelo, Associated Press
